name: Watching-eye effect
statement: A picture of eyes is said to make people behave better when nobody is really watching, from paying for coffee to dropping less litter.
meaning: The claim has two parts. The first is that humans carry machinery for detecting observation and adjusting conduct to protect a reputation. The second is that the machinery is crude enough to fire on a photograph. Nothing about a printed pair of eyes can carry information to anyone, so a person who gives more, litters less or steals less in front of one is responding to a cue that cannot possibly cost or reward them. That is what makes the finding interesting and what makes it fragile. The claim is separate from the effect of a real observer, which is the larger finding: people do behave differently when somebody can actually see them. Entry 26 covers the neighbouring claim that people change their behaviour because they know they are being studied.

origin.who: Kevin J. Haley and Daniel M. T. Fessler
origin.note: Their dictator-game paper, "Nobody's watching?", put stylised eyespots on a computer desktop and reported more giving. The demonstration that made the idea famous came a year later, when Bateson, Nettle and Roberts ran the honesty box in a Newcastle coffee room.

evidence: Bateson, Nettle and Roberts hung a notice above an honesty box in the coffee room of the Division of Psychology at Newcastle University. Its 150 by 35 millimetre banner alternated each week between a pair of eyes and an image of flowers, over ten weeks. Tea, coffee and milk cost 30, 50 and 10 pence. The paper describes a population of 48 members of the division, 25 women and 23 men, who had the option to pay, and it records no individual decisions. Milk consumption served as the index of how much was drunk. People paid 2.76 times as much per litre of milk in the eyes weeks, 0.417 pounds plus or minus 0.081 against 0.151 plus or minus 0.030. A general linear model on log-transformed data explained 63.8 percent of the variance, with a main effect of image type, F(1,7) = 11.551, p = 0.011, and no effect of week, F(1,7) = 0.074, p = 0.794. The unit of analysis was the week, so the result rests on ten numbers. Haley and Fessler's earlier dictator game used five conditions, combining a stylised image of eyes on the computer desktop with sound-deadening earmuffs meant to cut the sound of other people in the room. That paper was not obtained for this entry. Northover and colleagues, who pooled its three cue conditions against its two control conditions, put it at 124 participants and score it at Hedges' g = 0.30, 95% confidence interval -0.06 to 0.67 for the amount given, and a log odds ratio of 1.21, 95% CI 0.42 to 2.01, for the proportion who gave anything. Nettle and colleagues, replicating it in 2013, stress that two logically separable effects were present in the original: eyes raised the mean donation, and eyes also raised the probability of donating something rather than nothing.

examples.tag: The honesty box in the staff kitchen
examples.text: A tin for tea money sits under a poster. In the weeks when the poster shows a pair of eyes, more money goes in than in the weeks when it shows a plant. Nobody is checking either way, and the eyes on paper can report to no one.

A bottle bank with a face printed on the panel collects less rubbish dumped at its foot than the identical bank on the next estate. A photograph cannot see who left the bag, which is what makes the change odd rather than obvious.

examples.tag: The screen at the self-service till
examples.text: A checkout screen that shows a pair of eyes while items are scanned is followed by fewer unscanned items than one that shows a logo. The store is no better informed, since nothing about the picture records anything.

replication.headline: Pooled across 26 experiments, eye images moved the amount people gave by Hedges' g = 0.03; separate pools on antisocial behaviour and on whether a person gives anything at all report reductions and increases that hold.
replication.detail: Northover, Pedersen, Cohen and Andrews ran two meta-analyses on generosity in 2017. The first covered the mean amount given: 26 experiments, 2,732 participants, 18 papers of which one was unpublished, and 2 theses. The random-effects estimate was Hedges' g = 0.03, SE 0.05, 95% CI -0.08 to 0.13, with Q(25) = 40.81, p = .02. The second covered whether a person gave anything at all, the version of the claim Nettle and colleagues had argued for: 27 experiments, 19,512 participants, log odds ratio 0.16, SE 0.10, an odds ratio of 1.17, with an interval of -0.04 to 0.35 and Q(26) = 34.98, p = .11. A companion paper the same year ran two meta-analyses of six experiments each on moral judgement. The wallet vignette gave an unstandardised mean difference of -0.05, SE 0.18, 95% CI -0.40 to 0.30 on a nine-point scale across 1,350 participants; the resume vignette gave -0.21, SE 0.11, 95% CI -0.43 to -0.00003 across 1,346, which its own authors call barely significant. Nettle and colleagues had read a smaller pool the other way in 2013: seven dictator-game studies, 887 participants, a pooled d of 0.04, t(887) = 0.60, p = 0.55 for the amount given, and 79.4 percent donating something under eyes against 73.4 percent under control, Fisher's exact p = 0.04, an odds ratio of 1.39, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.91. Their own replication on 118 Newcastle students found the same split: no effect on the amount, F(1,114) = 0.03, p = 0.86, and an effect on whether anything was given, Wald chi-squared = 4.26, p = 0.04, 80 percent against 63 percent. Dear, Dutton and Fox pooled 15 experiments from 13 papers on antisocial behaviour rather than generosity, 2,035 participants. Leaving out three studies whose eye images carried explicit text, such as the 'Cycle Thieves We're Watching You' sign, their random-effects estimate was a log odds ratio of -0.45, SE 0.18, 95% CI -0.81 to -0.09, p = .01, an odds ratio of 0.64. Adding the three back, the random-effects estimate held at -0.43, SE 0.17, 95% CI -0.76 to -0.11, while the fixed-effects estimate fell to -0.13, SE 0.05, 95% CI -0.23 to -0.03, an odds ratio of 0.88. Two broader pools land in between. Bradley, Lawrence and Ferguson meta-analysed observability and prosociality across 117 papers, 134 study-level effects and 788,164 people, finding r = 0.141, for which their abstract gives a 95% interval of 0.106 to 0.175 and their results section 0.101 to 0.175. Their perceived-observability subgroup, the category defined to hold watching-eyes images, gave r = 0.100, 95% CI 0.050 to 0.149, k = 49, against r = 0.352, 95% CI 0.225 to 0.478, k = 12, for a live passive observer. Wang and colleagues pooled 216 effect sizes from 91 articles and report a log odds ratio of 0.231 and Hedges' g = 0.117, both of which they call significant.

study.cite: Northover, S. B., Pedersen, W. C., Cohen, A. B., & Andrews, P. W. (2017). Artificial surveillance cues do not increase generosity: two meta-analyses. Evolution and Human Behavior, 38(1), 144-153.

limits: The honesty box has not survived close inspection. Carbon and Hesslinger reran Bateson's own analysis and found the general linear model rested on unequal error variances, Bartlett's test chi-squared = 121.8, p < .0001. Repeating it uncorrected reproduced the published result, F(1,7) = 11.82, p = .011, partial eta squared 0.628. Correcting for the violated assumption left what they report as a non-significant result, F(2,7) = 4.56, p = .054. Of the four distribution tests they ran on the ten weekly figures, only the Mann-Whitney U reached significance, U = 1.0, Z = -2.402, p = .016. Their own laboratory experiment, 141 volunteers of whom 138 were analysed, found no effect of the social cue on any of four socially relevant scenarios, F(1,133) < 1, p = .5618. Nettle wrote on his own site in March 2022 that he knew of no attempt at a direct replication of the coffee room, positive or null, and that his group cannot run one because the kitchen no longer has an honesty box. What the original team did instead was move the design to other behaviours. Bateson, Robinson, Abayomi-Cole, Greenlees, O'Connor and Nettle attached leaflets to parked bicycles in two field experiments and found the eyes leaflets less likely to be littered, odds ratios 0.22 to 0.32. In the second experiment the eyes reduced littering only when nobody else was nearby, and littering was higher than control when somebody was. The moderators offered to rescue the effect have their own record. Sparks and Barclay proposed that eyes work only briefly, and their 188-participant dictator game found giving differing by condition, F(2,185) = 5.02, p = 0.008, with more under sudden eyespots than under constant ones, t(131) = 3.04, p = 0.003, though the contrast against no eyes reached only t(122) = 1.67, p = 0.049. Eight years later Sparks and Barclay were co-authors on a preregistered attempt with 355 students that found nothing: allocations did not differ by condition, F(2,353) = 1.02, p = .360, partial eta squared .006, and the eyes condition did not leave participants feeling more observed than the control. Oda argues the other way, that the null meta-analyses pooled classroom surveys and online labour markets with controlled laboratory sessions, and so passed over how many real people were nearby. He writes that it is uncertain what removing those studies would do, and offers no reanalysis. Dear and colleagues' own set is small and uneven: of 15 experiments, one corruption experiment carries a log odds ratio of -1.78 and four point the other way, the largest being engine idling at 0.63. They call their foundations narrow and say it would be premature to place much weight on them. Heterogeneity in the wider literature is extreme; Bradley and colleagues report I-squared of 99.24.
misreadings: The 2.76 figure is the most quoted number in this literature and the least transferable. It is one coffee room, one department, ten weekly observations, and money per litre of milk rather than per person. Dear, Dutton and Fox left that study out of their meta-analysis for that reason, because it counted neither how much individuals donated nor how many of them did. The second error is treating the two meta-analytic camps as if they answered the same question. Northover and colleagues pooled generosity in economic games and donation tasks, and found nothing. Dear, Dutton and Fox pooled littering, dishonesty, corruption, bicycle theft and engine idling, and found a reduction. Neither pool contains the honesty box, a point Nettle presses against readings of Northover's result as a verdict on his coffee room. The third error involves Sparks and Barclay's 2013 paper, widely cited as a meta-analysis confirming the effect at short exposures. Its meta-analysis counts published outcomes rather than pooling effect sizes: it classified 25 experiments by whether any effect was reported and by exposure length, then ran Fisher's exact tests on the resulting table, with 15 of 16 short-exposure studies reporting an effect and none of 5 prolonged-exposure studies doing so, p < 0.005. A vote count of published outcomes is the design most exposed to whatever kept the null results out of print. Fourth, Nettle and colleagues' formulation, that eyes change whether you give rather than how much, is often cited as the surviving version of the effect. Their own pool of seven studies put it at an odds ratio of 1.39, and Northover's second meta-analysis tested the same formulation on 19,512 people and got an interval that crossed zero. Fifth, none of this touches the effect of a real observer. Bradley and colleagues put a live passive observer at r = 0.352 against r = 0.100 for a cue that only implies observation, and the gap between those two numbers is the whole subject.
